title: Control Theory
description: How feedback makes machines hold a target: block diagrams, response shapes, PID, stability and tuning.
audience: Adults who have studied introductory calculus and mechanics. No Laplace transforms required.
outcomes: You'll be able to reduce a feedback loop to one gain.
You'll be able to read and compute first and second order responses.
You'll be able to explain and tune P, I and D terms.
You'll be able to test a loop for stability.

sources.licence: Free electronic edition; copyright Princeton University Press

lessons.title: Why close the loop
lessons.objective: Explain what feedback buys over open-loop control and compute its effect on gain error.

concepts.title: Loop parts
concepts.summary: A feedback loop has a plant, a sensor, a comparison with a target and a controller acting on the error.

concepts.title: Sensitivity
concepts.summary: Feedback shrinks the effect of plant changes and disturbances on the output, at the cost of loop gain being spent.

misconceptions: Learners think feedback removes error. With proportional feedback a finite error remains.
Learners think a thermostat computes how long to heat. It only compares and switches.
Learners think open loop is always worse; it is cheaper and fine when the plant is known and disturbances small.
sequence: A toaster timer versus a thermostat.
Name plant, sensor, setpoint, error, controller, actuator, disturbance.
A plant with gain 2 and open-loop scaling 0.5.
The same plant when its gain falls 20 percent: open loop falls 20 percent.
Closed loop with controller gain 8: output = KG/(1+KG).
Loop gain is the currency feedback spends.
examples: Plant gain 2, controller gain 0.5 open loop: output 1.0. Plant gain falls to 1.6: output 0.8, down 20 percent.
Closed loop, K=8: 16/17=0.941; with G=1.6: 12.8/13.8=0.9275, down only 1.45 percent.
The remaining 5.9 percent error is the price of finite gain.

lessons.title: Block diagrams and reducing a loop
lessons.objective: Reduce series, parallel and feedback blocks to a single gain.

concepts.title: Combining blocks
concepts.summary: Blocks in series multiply; a feedback loop of forward gain G and feedback gain H gives G/(1+GH).

concepts.title: Sign convention
concepts.summary: Negative feedback subtracts the measurement at the summing junction.

misconceptions: Learners add the gains of blocks in series instead of multiplying.
Learners write G/(1 - G H) for negative feedback; that is the formula for positive feedback.
Learners drop H when it is 1 and then forget it when it is not.
sequence: Show the symbols: a block multiplies, an arrow carries a signal, a circle adds or subtracts, a dot splits.
Two blocks in series multiply: signal 1 through gains 2 and 3 becomes 6.
Two blocks in parallel into a summing junction add.
Derive feedback: y = G e and e = r - H y, so y = G r - G H y, giving y/r = G/(1 + G H).
Reduce a three-block diagram step by step, inner loop first.
Check the sign at each junction before trusting the result.
examples: Series 2 and 3 then unity feedback: 6/7=0.857.
Positive feedback with G=0.5, H=1: 0.5/(1-0.5)=1.

lessons.title: First-order response
lessons.objective: Describe and compute the step response of a first-order system from its time constant.

concepts.title: Time constant
concepts.summary: The time for a first-order step response to cover 63.2 percent of the way to its final value.

concepts.title: Rate proportional to gap
concepts.summary: tau dy/dt = K u - y says the output closes the gap to its target at a rate proportional to the gap.

misconceptions: Learners expect the output to reach the final value at time tau. It reaches 63 percent.
Learners think the response ends. It is never exactly final, so settling is defined by a percent.
Learners confuse the time constant with the delay.
sequence: A cooling cup of coffee: rate depends on the gap.
Write tau dy/dt = K u - y.
Solve: y = K u (1 - e^(-t/tau)).
Checkpoints: 63, 86, 95, 98, 99 percent at 1 to 5 tau.
Initial slope = final/tau.
RC circuit and thermal examples.
examples: RC with 10 kilohm and 100 microfarad: tau=1 s.
Sensor tau=8 s: 90 percent at 8 ln 10=18.4 s; 95 percent at 24.0 s.
At t=2 tau the response is 1-e^-2=0.865.

figures.shows: First-order step response with horizontal guide lines at 63 and 95 percent and a tangent at the origin.
RC circuit and its voltage curve.

questionPlan.sample: tau=8 s. Time to 90 percent in seconds to 1 decimal?

lessons.title: A first-order plant in a loop
lessons.objective: Compute the closed-loop time constant and final value for proportional control of a first-order plant.

concepts.title: Closed-loop time constant
concepts.summary: tau_cl = tau/(1+K Kp): more gain makes it faster.

concepts.title: Steady-state error
concepts.summary: The final value is K Kp/(1+K Kp), always less than 1 for finite gain.

misconceptions: Learners think more gain only improves things; a lag in the loop can later cause overshoot.
Learners think the plant's tau is unchangeable; feedback shifts it.
Learners think zero error is possible with P alone.
sequence: Start from tau dy/dt = -y + K u with u = Kp (r - y).
Rearrange to the same form with tau_cl.
Compute tau_cl and the final value.
Plot for Kp = 1, 4, 16.
The error shrinks as 1/(1+L).
Next: remove the error with integral action.
examples: tau=10 s, K=2, Kp=4: loop gain 8, tau_cl=10/9=1.11 s, final 8/9=0.889, error 11.1 percent.
Kp=16: loop gain 32, tau_cl=0.30 s, final 32/33=0.970.
Kp=0 gives no motion.

figures.shows: Step responses for several Kp values on the same axes.
A loop simulation with Euler steps.

Euler: y=0; repeat 100 times dt=0.1: u=4*(1-y); y += dt*(-y+2*u)/10. Print y rounded to 3 places.

lessons.title: Second-order response
lessons.objective: Compute natural frequency, damping ratio, overshoot and timing for a mass-spring-damper.

concepts.title: Damping ratio
concepts.summary: zeta = c/(2 sqrt(k m)): below 1 the response overshoots and rings; at 1 it is critical.

concepts.title: Overshoot
concepts.summary: Peak overshoot Mp = exp(-pi zeta / sqrt(1 - zeta^2)).

misconceptions: Learners think damping slows the response. A lightly damped system takes longer to settle.
Learners read frequency as speed. Natural frequency sets the scale; damping shapes the response.
Learners think critical damping is always best; it is slowest to rise without overshoot.
sequence: Mass-spring-damper: m x'' + c x' + k x = F.
wn = sqrt(k/m); zeta.
Underdamped, critical, overdamped.
Overshoot depends only on zeta.
Settling time about 4/(zeta wn).
Peak time pi/(wn sqrt(1-zeta^2)).
examples: m=2 kg, k=800 N/m, c=40 N s/m: wn=20 rad/s, zeta=0.5, overshoot 16.3 percent, settling 0.40 s, peak time 0.181 s.
zeta=0.2: overshoot 52.7 percent.
Critical damping needs c=2 sqrt(k m)=80 N s/m.

figures.shows: Second-order step responses for zeta 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2.
A mass on a spring with a damper, drawn beside its step response.

historyNotes: Maxwell's 1868 paper 'On Governors' was the first mathematical stability analysis of a feedback device.

lessons.title: Designing to a specification
lessons.objective: Turn overshoot and settling limits into limits on damping and frequency.

concepts.title: Time-domain specifications
concepts.summary: Rise time, overshoot, settling time and steady-state error describe a step response.

concepts.title: Damping from overshoot
concepts.summary: zeta = -ln(Mp) / sqrt(pi^2 + ln^2 Mp).

misconceptions: Learners try to satisfy all specs at once without trade-offs.
Learners use overshoot to fix wn; overshoot fixes zeta only.
Learners add 5 percent to the final value for settling.
sequence: Mark rise time, overshoot, settling time and steady-state error on a step response plot.
Overshoot depends only on damping ratio: invert Mp = exp(-pi z/sqrt(1-z^2)) to get z = -ln Mp / sqrt(pi^2 + ln^2 Mp).
Settling time (2 percent) is about 4/(z wn), so a limit on it sets z wn.
Rise time is about 1.8/wn for moderate damping, so a limit on it sets wn.
Combine the limits into a region of acceptable z and wn.
Meet the box and note what it cost: faster responses ask more of the actuator.
examples: Mp <= 10 percent: zeta >= 0.591.
Mp <= 5 percent: zeta >= 0.690.
Settling <= 2 s with zeta 0.6: wn >= 4/(0.6*2)=3.33 rad/s.

figures.shows: Step response with spec band and shaded forbidden zone.
Specs to parameters.

questionPlan.sample: Overshoot limit 10 percent. Minimum zeta to 2 decimals?
Settling 2 s, zeta 0.5. Minimum wn in rad/s?

lessons.title: Proportional control and droop
lessons.objective: Compute steady-state error under proportional control and the gain needed for a target.

concepts.title: Proportional term
concepts.summary: u = Kp e: action proportional to the current error.

concepts.title: Steady-state error
concepts.summary: For a plant with DC gain G0, a unit step leaves e = 1/(1 + Kp G0).

misconceptions: Learners expect error to vanish with high gain.
Learners expect Kp to react to history; it does not.
Learners think a disturbance is a different matter. It shifts the offset.
sequence: Define u = Kp e: action proportional to the present error.
Ask what the plant needs to hold the target: a nonzero control u.
A nonzero u needs a nonzero e, so P-only control must leave an error: e = 1/(1 + Kp G0) for a unit step.
Raise Kp to shrink the error, and see the cost in noise and overshoot.
Add a constant disturbance and show it moves the offset.
Conclude with the question integral action answers.
examples: G0=5, Kp=3: loop gain 15, ess=1/16=6.25 percent.
Target ess <= 2 percent: loop gain >= 49, Kp >= 9.8.
A heater needs 30 percent power to hold temperature; the error that produces it never goes to zero.

Heater with required hold power.

lessons.title: Integral action
lessons.objective: Compute an integral term, explain why it removes offset, and anticipate windup.

concepts.title: Integral term
concepts.summary: Ki times the accumulated error, which keeps growing until the error is gone.

concepts.title: Windup
concepts.summary: When the actuator saturates the integral keeps growing and must be unwound later.

misconceptions: Learners think the integral acts on the current error only.
Learners think integral action always improves the response; it adds lag and risk of oscillation.
Learners ignore saturation.
sequence: Define the integral term as Ki times the area under the error curve so far.
Add up a short list of errors by rectangles.
Explain why the output can only settle when the error is zero: otherwise the integral still moves.
Show a PI loop on the heater removing the offset.
Show windup: actuator at its limit, integral growing.
Fix windup by stopping the integral at saturation.
examples: Errors 1.0, 0.6, 0.3, 0.1 at dt 0.5: sum*dt=1.0; Ki=2 gives 2.0.
PI on the first-order plant (Kp 4, Ki 0.8): final value 1.000 in 100 s.
Saturated for 10 s at error 20: integral 200; unwinding at error -10 takes 20 s.

figures.shows: Output, error and integral term traces.
PI loop simulation.

lessons.title: Derivative action and the full PID
lessons.objective: Compute a PID output and explain what derivative action buys and costs.

concepts.title: Derivative term
concepts.summary: Kd de/dt acts on the rate of change, damping approach before overshoot.

concepts.title: Noise amplification
concepts.summary: Derivative action multiplies high-frequency noise by 2 pi f.

misconceptions: Learners think D predicts the future accurately; it extrapolates linearly.
Learners apply derivative to a setpoint step and get a spike.
Learners think more D is always safe.
sequence: Add a term on the slope of the error: Kd de/dt.
Think of it as a brake: it pushes against fast motion before the target is passed.
Assemble the full u = Kp e + Ki integral(e) + Kd de/dt and compute one value.
Show noise: a small fast wiggle has a large slope.
Fix noise with a filter and take the derivative of the measurement.
Say when each term earns its place.
examples: Noise 0.01 at 50 Hz: derivative 2 pi 50 0.01=3.14 per s; with Kd=0.1 it adds 0.31.
Setpoint step in e makes a spike if derivative acts on e.

figures.shows: Three traces of response with D added.
PID block diagram.

lessons.title: Stability
lessons.objective: Decide the range of gain over which a loop is stable and find where it oscillates.

concepts.title: Stable
concepts.summary: Every disturbance dies away: all characteristic roots have negative real parts.

concepts.title: Cubic test
concepts.summary: s^3 + a2 s^2 + a1 s + a0 is stable if all coefficients are positive and a2 a1 > a0.

misconceptions: Learners think a large gain is always better.
Learners think instability means the output goes up smoothly; it often oscillates growing.
Learners think the plant alone being stable makes the loop stable.
sequence: Solutions e^(st): roots decide decay.
Negative real part decays; imaginary part rings.
Quadratic: positive coefficients.
Cubic condition.
Example s^3+3s^2+2s+K.
Critical gain and frequency.
examples: K: stable for 0 < K < 6; at K=6 roots s=-3 and s=+/-j sqrt 2.
Ultimate period Tu=2 pi/sqrt 2=4.44 s.
Quadratic s^2+4s+5: roots -2 +/- j, stable.

figures.shows: Complex plane with draggable root and the matching time response.
Step responses for K = 1, 4, 6, 8.

historyNotes: Edward Routh published his criterion in 1877 and Adolf Hurwitz independently in 1895.

lessons.title: Tuning a PID
lessons.objective: Set PID gains using the closed-loop and reaction-curve methods.

concepts.title: Ultimate-gain method
concepts.summary: Raise Kp until steady oscillation; then P=0.5Ku, PI=0.45Ku, PID=0.6Ku, Ti=Tu/2, Td=Tu/8.

concepts.title: Reaction-curve method
concepts.summary: From a step test fit gain K, delay L and time constant T, then PID Kp=1.2T/(K L), Ti=2L, Td=0.5L.

misconceptions: Learners treat Ziegler-Nichols as optimal; it is a starting point with about 25 percent overshoot.
Learners tune D first, which amplifies noise.
Learners tune a live process without limits on the actuator.
sequence: Rules of thumb exist because models are often unavailable.
Method 1: raise Kp until the output holds a steady oscillation; record Ku and Tu.
Convert to PID settings with Kp = 0.6 Ku, Ti = Tu/2, Td = Tu/8.
Method 2: a step test gives gain K, delay L and time constant T; use Kp = 1.2 T/(K L), Ti = 2L, Td = 0.5 L.
Judge the response: these settings give lively responses, often 25 percent overshoot, so detune.
Tune by hand: P first, then I, then a little D.

lessons.title: Real loops: limits, sampling and feedforward
lessons.objective: Handle actuator limits, sample time and feedforward in a working loop.

concepts.title: Anti-windup
concepts.summary: Stop integrating while the output is saturated.

concepts.title: Feedforward
concepts.summary: Command the expected control from the setpoint so feedback only fixes the remainder.

misconceptions: Learners assume a controller tuned in continuous time will behave the same when sampled slowly.
Learners think feedforward replaces feedback; it handles what the model knows, feedback handles the rest.
Learners ignore actuator limits until windup appears.
sequence: Controllers run in samples: choose a period of at most a tenth of the rise time.
Write the discrete PID: error each step, sum for the integral, difference for the derivative.
Actuators saturate; stop integrating when the output is clamped.
Feedforward: command the expected control from the setpoint, so feedback only trims.
Sensor noise: filter the measurement before the derivative.
Safety: a limit, a timeout and a safe output on sensor failure.
examples: Rise time 2 s: sample at most every 0.2 s.
Plant gain 2, target 6: feedforward u=3.
Valve limit 100 percent: clamp the integral.
